platforms.title: 3 Signs Rectal Bleeding Is a Fissure, Not Hemorrhoids
platforms.meta_description: Seeing blood after a bowel movement doesn't always mean hemorrhoids. How to tell an anal fissure apart by its pain pattern, and when to see a doctor.
platforms.body_html:
Notice blood on the toilet paper or in the bowl and assume it's just hemorrhoids? The American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons explains that hemorrhoids and anal fissures are completely different conditions with different causes and pain patterns. Both are common, but which one is actually going on changes what actually helps.

Why the pain feels so different between the two

Hemorrhoids are swollen blood vessels in or around the anus, usually from straining during bowel movements, pregnancy, prolonged sitting, chronic constipation or diarrhea, and supporting tissue weakening with age. They typically show up as painless, bright red blood that coats the stool or drips into the toilet. An anal fissure, on the other hand, is a small tear in the lining of the anal canal, usually caused by passing a hard or unusually large stool. It produces a sharp pain during and after the bowel movement, often described as passing glass, lasting minutes to hours, and the blood is usually a smaller amount, streaked on the surface of the stool.

According to the American Society of Colon and Rectal Surgeons, the biggest risk factors for hemorrhoids are constipation, pregnancy, obesity, prolonged sitting or straining, and age, while fissures are linked to constipation with hard stools, childbirth, and chronic diarrhea.

How to tell them apart, and when it's time to see a doctor

First, whether it hurts. Hemorrhoids are usually painless, sometimes with itching or a bulge, while a fissure causes clear, sharp pain with each bowel movement.

Second, the color of the blood and whether the bleeding is changing. Blood that isn't bright red, or bleeding that keeps increasing, unexplained weight loss, or new bleeding after age 45 with a family history of colon cancer are not something to write off as ordinary hemorrhoids or a fissure — they call for a colonoscopy or a proper evaluation.

For both, getting enough fiber and fluids to keep stool soft is the basic first step. Warm sitz baths and topical treatments help too. Most fissures heal within a few weeks with this kind of care, but a hemorrhoid that's clotted and swollen, or a fissure that won't heal, may need a procedure.

A doctor can usually confirm which one it is with a quick physical exam, since a fissure is often visible right at the edge of the anus and hemorrhoids have a fairly distinctive look and location of their own. What's worth mentioning specifically at that appointment is how long the pain lasts after a bowel movement, since a fissure's sharp pain tends to linger for a while afterward in a way ordinary hemorrhoid discomfort usually doesn't. Bringing a rough sense of how often the bleeding happens, whether it's getting better or worse, and any change in bowel habits gives a doctor far more to work with than trying to describe it all from memory on the spot.

The takeaway: check whether it hurts before assuming any blood after a bowel movement is just hemorrhoids. Unusual color, increasing blood, or other symptoms mean it's worth having a doctor check. This article is for general health information; consult a medical professional for diagnosis and treatment.
